content.thinking:
I need to plan out the whole file carefully upfront since I won't be testing as I go, so I'm thinking through realistic proportions for a red panda balanced on a mossy stone—body, tail, and stance sized to match real-world scale while keeping the pose natural rather than mid-action.

For the Genshin-style flourishes, I'm keeping it restrained: a small gold bell collar with tassel and a glowing dendro seed pendant, rather than piling on too many glowing effects.

Now I'm working out the actual skeleton coordinates—stone height, body length and radius, hip and shoulder positions, and how the legs connect from hip joints down to the feet resting on the stone's surface.

I'm calculating limb proportions so the knee and elbow bends look natural: using two-segment legs with the hind knees bending forward and front elbows bending back, adjusting segment lengths so the stance lifts the body with a visible, believable joint angle.

For the paw placement, I'm making the feet rest flat on the stone top with a slight moss layer, and setting up the joint chains (hip, knee, ankle) so each limb gets a proper tip joint. I'm also deciding to work directly in world coordinates, so the left side is simply +X, and now I'm setting up the spine as a chain rooted at the hips.

Defining spine, neck, and head joints...

For the body coloring, I'm setting up a countershading scheme wrapped in a cel shader to capture the red panda's rusty red back against dark chestnut belly and legs, plus the white face markings and ringed tail.

Still defining fur colors...

Now I'm working out the head geometry: a broad red panda skull sphere scaled for wide cheeks, with joints for head and jaw placed at specific model-space coordinates. I'm planning the facial markings next -- white muzzle, cheeks, eyebrow patches, and dark tear streaks -- using paint functions tied to model-space positions.

Simplifying the tear stripe region, then wrapping the whole head paint in a cel-shading function that uses the surface normal for lighting and shadow. For the eyes, I'll add a decal on the skull with an amber iris color.

I'm placing the eye decal by finding the surface hit point on the skull at a given azimuth and elevation, then applying it with mirroring based on side, using a wide/tall size for the big anime-eye look.

Now I'm sketching the muzzle: a scaled sphere for the short snout in cream paint, a tiny dark sphere for the nose tip, and a smaller cream sphere for the lower jaw attached to the jaw bone, plus considering a small pink tongue and a smile line swept in ink under the nose.

I'll use a surface-draping technique so the mouth and philtrum curves hug the muzzle's surface instead of floating, placing rough points near the muzzle front and letting the drape lift them slightly off the skin.

For the ears, I'm planning red panda-style rounded triangular shapes with a white rim and cream fluff, extruding a smoothed outline and tilting the ear plane outward using non-orthogonal x/y basis vectors so they angle naturally from the head.

I'm layering several extrusions at offset depths to build the rust-colored back, cream rim, and dark inner tuft, adjusting thickness and z-shifts so each layer peeks out correctly behind the next.

For the cheeks, I'm adding small cream cone tufts angled outward from each side of the head to give the fluffy ruff look.

For face details, I'm sketching white eyebrow patches as cream marks painted directly onto the head geometry above the eyes, and planning thin cream whisker rods extending from the muzzle sides using a low-segment spike shape.

I'm also considering a small glowing leaf-shaped emissive mark on the forehead for a dendro-style elemental accent, plus a gold neck collar with a bell, tassel, and glowing seed, built as a sweep loop around the neck joint.

For the skeleton structure, I'm working out whether spine and neck should be one continuous catmull path or two separate chains—settling on a spine chain from rump to withers, with a neck chain parented off the last spine joint, then combining both into a single "body" sweep path.

I'm now sketching out the actual coordinates along that body path from rump through withers to the neck midpoint, defining the counts for each chain (spine: 4 joints, neck: 2) so the joint naming works out automatically.

Now I'm defining the body radius profile along its spine path, tapering from the rump through the widest middle section, narrowing at the withers, and thinning further into the neck, so the sweep can shape the coat mesh accordingly.

For the belly paint, I'll use a mottled rust tone with a cel-shaded fuzzy edge against the body, giving it a slightly darker chestnut shade for contrast with the lighter shoulders.

Now I'm thinking through fur tufts as flame-shaped SVG cards scattered across the body, filtered to avoid the belly region, with randomized size, lean, and bend so they flow backward naturally, tinted to match the main coat color rather than drawn in fixed hues.

Next I'm planning the tail: a bushy, ring-patterned structure alternating rust and darker bands, curved upward in an S shape to give it a raised, dynamic pose.

I'm plotting a 5-joint chain for the tail from the hip back, calculating segment lengths and rescaling the curve since my first path came out around 0.75m, too long — real red panda tails run closer to 0.45-0.5m relative to a 0.52m body.

Still refining the tail chain...

I'll make the ring boundaries wavy by zigzagging based on angle, then scatter tail tuft elements along the tail sweep with minimum spacing and a slight lean.

For the tail flow direction, since the tail points upward, I need the fur to flatten backward against the tail's surface -- I'll approximate with a flow vector pointing down and back rather than computing exact tangents.

Now I'm working on leg coloring with a dark chestnut-black base and a rust-to-dark gradient near the hip blending down to the knee, then adding black paws with small rounded toe bumps and tiny claws, positioning the feet to rest naturally on the stone surface.

I'm figuring out foot and hip placement for the fore and hind limbs, adding a thigh/haunch bulge at the hip for a fuller silhouette, and setting up the limb chain so the hip-to-foot line bends correctly in the right plane.

Working through limb bend geometry: for the hind legs I'm orienting the knee to bow forward, checking the hip-to-foot distance against segment lengths to make sure the offset is solvable, and doing the same calculation for the forelegs with the elbow bending backward. I'm now starting to build the leg chain structure with hip-named joints and a parent reference.

Still deciding how to pick parents for each leg chain and name the joints by side, then setting up the sweep radii that taper from hip to ankle. I'm also starting to think about building the mossy stone base, considering a lumpy multi-piece shape rather than a simple lathe.

Adding more boulder shapes...

I'm widening the stone's lathe profile so the panda feet sit on the slope correctly, then stretching it along z using a scale factor since lathe shapes need elongating to fit the body proportions. I'm checking whether Part supports painting lathe geometry in model space so colors apply correctly.

Now I'm sinking the stone slightly below the floor to avoid a visible seam, then planning the paint logic for a mossy, cracked stone surface with blue-gray coloring and green moss patches near the top, inspired by Genshin's art style.

I'm defining a zigzag-edged moss boundary function that blends noise and mottled stone coloring under cel shading for a painterly texture, then scattering small moss tuft cards across the top surface while filtering out the area directly under the panda's footprint so they don't poke through its paws.

For dendro flavor, I'm skipping any floating decals or glowing rune circles and instead adding grounded elements -- a leaf-shaped dendro seed pendant on the collar, a forehead mark, glowing flower stems, and glowing mushrooms on the stone, keeping everything touching the surface as required. Now I'm working out the collar loop placement, anchoring it to a joint along the neck chain and orienting the loop plane to face that joint's axis.

I'm sweeping the collar loop into a gold-painted tube, then deciding to add a small bell and tassel at the front under the chin for a Genshin-style touch -- working through how to compute the correct ray direction from the neck's center point so the bell lands on the front-facing surface rather than hitting the chest incorrectly.

Still placing tassel and pendant geometry...

PathPoint frames carry weight info, so using b.part with the at parameter should work fine for placing studs along the collar. Now I'm thinking about a forehead dendro mark—a small leaf-shaped emissive outline positioned near the top front of the skull.

Working out where the leaf should sit, I'm computing the surface point at the top of the skull by solving for the z-extent given the y-offset, then figuring out the tangent direction so the extrude orientation follows the curvature correctly, using the hit/skin approach to get the right placement and local axes.

Eyes sit around elevation 3. For the head paint, I'm thinking through how the skull sphere part uses model-space coordinates, so cheek markings need to account for that scaling—red pandas have cream/white cheek fur, so I'm marking the lower cheeks cream in the paint layer.

Now I'm working out exact head joint positions: the head bone sits around z=.29 with the skull center offset forward to z=.355, and the neck path terminates around the same area. I'm considering making the head slightly larger relative to the body for that classic chibi big-head proportion, adjusting radii to roughly [0.105, 0.09, 0.095] and introducing a scale constant to keep eye and muzzle offsets consistent.

Working through ear placement and orientation now -- defining chunky rounded ear outlines, deciding where the base sinks into the skull, and checking that the local coordinate axes for the ear extrusion stay orthogonal so the shape doesn't skew unexpectedly.

For the fur layering on the ears, I'm sequencing colors to mimic real red panda ears: a cream rim layer with rust showing behind it, building up thickness and offsets so the edges read as a light fringe around a darker base.

I'm also working out muzzle and eye placement relative to head scale, sizing the snout to protrude slightly beyond the skull front and positioning the nose sphere with a flattened vertical radius for a cuter look.

For the jaw, I'm placing a lower jaw bone beneath the muzzle with cream coloring and considering whether to skip the tongue since the mouth stays closed. I'm also figuring out where the smile sweep should drape on the muzzle surface so it doesn't get hidden by the jaw overlap, adjusting the y-coordinates slightly upward to keep it visible.

Writing whisker geometry...

Then I'm adding cheek tufts as small cream spikes radiating from the head, and considering whether cream should use a shared cel paint rather than flat colors for palette efficiency. I'm deciding to skip extra fur cards and chest shading since the red panda body stays dark with only the face in white/cream.

Now I'm designing a tiny flower hairpin ornament for the ear, using a ring of five petal spheres around a gold center, positioned near the ear base and angled outward-forward with a pink cel tint. I'm working through how the ring frame and bone inheritance should work for these petal items.

Separately, I'm sketching SVG tuft textures (rust-colored feather tufts with cream and dark variants, plus moss and flower assets) and planning how to scatter tufts along the tail sweep with specific density, size, and bend parameters so they lean and flow toward the tip.

For the tail tufts, I'm randomizing between rust and dark textures for ring coloring, which should read fine since variation is acceptable. I'm also working out facial details like anime-style eyes with tear/blush markings, using distance-based conditions from the eye center to paint a tear stripe running down the cheek.

Now I'm defining the cream cheek and brow regions using position offsets from the head center, wrapping the whole paint function in a cel-shading pass, and sketching out a cheek line formula that blends cream coloring outward using a zigzag pattern based on z-position.

I'm settling on the color palette: rust tones for the body, dark brown for legs/belly, cream for underside, and a darker reddish tear mark, plus stone and moss colors for the base. Then I'm planning the tail rings via a chain-sourced paint function, and scattering small rocks and grass blade cards around the stone base near ground level, keeping their roots at y=0 so nothing clips below the floor.

Now I'm figuring out placement for small glowing flowers on the stone's top edge, checking the ellipse math to make sure they land clear of the panda's feet, and sketching a flower-building function with a thin stem sweep, petal ring, and glowing gold center, while thinking through which bone to attach the stone parts to.

Attaching static props like the stone is tricky since my nearest-joint heuristic would parent it to a leg or spine joint and make it move with poses, which is wrong. I'm considering adding a dedicated static "base" root joint separate from "hips" so the stone stays fixed while the rig's hips can still move independently underneath it.

Placing a gold rune decal onto the stone's front face, figuring out the right projection position and size so it sits flush against the curved surface near the top.

Setting the decal target at the stone's surface normal, I work out the lathe profile points for the stone shape going bottom to top so normals face outward correctly, then add some irregular boulder lumps using flat-shaded icosahedron bumps embedded into the stone's side for a more natural look. I also double-check decal placement options for the skull eyes before moving on to writing the actual code.

Now I'm verifying API details for chains and surfaces — how `b.surface().around().at()` returns hits, how `b.chain()` builds a joint path with parent/count/role options, and confirming the spine-to-neck bone coat and hips-to-tail parenting line up correctly. I'm also checking the sweep radius keyframes along the body path and tail path, and making sure the tail ring coloring uses the right paint source over the tail chain.

Now I'm figuring out which imports I actually need (THREE, builder, frame, rng, catmull, limb, paint utilities, toon kit pieces, glow) to avoid unused-import errors, and setting up the limb import to generate joint points for a path. Writing imports and meta definition...

I'm defining the palette colors for rust, cream, gold, and other fur tones, then constructing layered paint functions—wrapping mottle and gradient textures inside furEdge and cel to get a toon-shaded, outlined coat material for the body, legs, and tail, while skipping heavy ink darkening to keep the look bright.

Now I'm writing the tail's banded pattern, alternating rust and dark-rust stripes based on a periodic zigzag of the surface angle, confirming that the cel shading correctly resolves these nested paint functions using the current surface sample. I'm then moving on to the stone material, blending two bluish-gray tones with a mottled noise pattern and edge highlighting.

For the stone, I'm adding a moss cap on upward-facing normals using layered noise thresholds, then considering adding dark crack lines using cellular noise where distance-field gaps are small. Now I'm starting the actual build function, setting up the skeleton with a base joint and hip joint using positional and directional offsets.

I'm defining the stone body as a lathe geometry generated from a rounded profile curve, scaled slightly to be more oval, and checking that the normals face outward correctly. I'm also considering adding small puffy moss mounds and boulder-like lumps on the rim using squashed spheres for extra texture.

Writing rock placement code...

Setting hind feet and tail root positions, then placing hip joints and haunch spheres with reused rust-colored fur material.

Now I'm building the leg chains for each side using limb bend directions, naming the hip/knee/ankle joints, and sweeping tapered radii along each chain before assigning the leg paint material and starting the paw joint.

I'm placing the paw as a flattened sphere at the foot joint, adding three small toe spheres with spike-shaped claws for texture, and setting dark chest coloring for the paws. I mirror this setup for the forelegs with reversed bend direction, note the fore paw target position, and then move on to defining a head coordinate helper function that scales offsets for placing ears and other features relative to the head center.

Now I'm building the skull geometry at the head joint, then writing a normalized paint function to classify surface points for eye placement using scaled distance thresholds. I'm using the surface helper to find symmetric eye positions around the skull, decaling them with mirroring, then setting up the cream muzzle part and sculpting a smile path by draping a catmull curve across the muzzle surface and sweeping it into a thin groove.

Now I'm scattering body tufts across the surface, filtering out points facing downward so they don't poke into the legs, then generating colored card clusters with randomized lean, bend, and spin for a furry texture, and considering adding similar cream tuft cards along the cheek ruff.

I'm also planning tail and grass cards, and deciding how to handle glow effects on flower centers versus skipping fireflies entirely. For the collar, I'm thinking through slicing a loop from the body sweep near the neck joint and extruding it into a thin gold ring to sit like a collar.

Adding stud spheres...

I'm working out the bell attachment, placing it at a specific point on the collar loop with slight embedding, then adding a hanging tassel cord using a spike shape with red coloring at an offset below the bell.

For the gem, I'm setting an octahedron shape positioned just above the bell on its own hit point, stretched vertically for a faceted look, making sure it's spaced apart from the bell so they don't overlap given the collar's radius.

Now I'm scattering moss tufts across the stone surface using card-style textures with random sizing and lean angles, then setting up grass blades around the base of the stone by computing positions along an elliptical radius at the ground level.

I'm defining each grass blade's frame with an outward-facing direction computed from its position, binding it to the correct bone so it follows the stone rather than snapping to the nearest joint, and sizing the green blade textures.

For the flowers, I'm building a stem as a thin four-sided rod rising from the ground, then arranging five petals in a ring around the stem's top using small sphere shapes...

Now I'm placing moss mounds along the stone's rim, picking several symmetric coordinates that stay within the elliptical boundary and avoid overlapping the panda, and checking the overall model height to confirm nothing between the ears, tail, and flowers exceeds a reasonable bound before reconsidering the tail's root position relative to the hips.

Still defining tail curve points...

Now I'm verifying the tail's radii taper and making sure the path stays clear of the stone's surface, then checking that the neck's bone chain resamples into the right number of named joints and that the spine naming convention produces sequential joint labels.

Writing joint and bone chain setup...

I'm placing the nose geometry with a small scaled sphere and a dark color, noting the eyes already include lash detail so no extra inner-mouth geometry is needed.

Writing the ear outline extrusion code, making sure the point tuples are typed correctly and the bevel settings won't break on the convex shape...

Setting base scale k to 1.2, then working out the cheek ruff spikes positioned around the head with directional offsets and sizing.

Placing three spikes at slightly different base points with a cream/bone coloring, and considering whether to add a small gold tail ring band as an extra decorative touch.

Adding toe bumps and tiny claw spikes to the paws, checking joint types and color functions, and sketching the leaf mark outline coordinates.

I need to be careful typing these mixed-tuple arrays explicitly so TypeScript doesn't choke on inference, so I'll annotate the leaf and ear outlines with the OutlinePoint type. After that it's just writing out the remaining SVG textures—rune marks, moss blades, and the various tuft color variants—plus double-checking the stick function signature and strict-mode variable usage before finishing the file.

Working through body proportions now: sweep radii along the spine, the fur edge darkening threshold on the belly, and teeth zigzag patterns, confirming they all mesh correctly where the neck meets the head. I'm also setting up the joint parenting for legs and spine, defining a typed tuple constant for head color, and placing a rune decal onto the stone bone with its position, direction, and size.

The stone placement checks out near the body profile radius at that height, so I'm satisfied it's positioned correctly on the surface. Ready to finalize and write it all out.
